281.title: The valley of Hunayn
281.hook: the army, proud of its numbers, nearly breaks at Hunayn (9:25)
281.howItsDone: Muslims recite 9:25–26 when warning against trusting in numbers or wealth, and the calm, sakinah, sent down at Hunayn is a word many use for the peace they ask God for in hard moments.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bilal: the man once crushed under a rock called the prayer from the top of the Ka'ba. Your line was bilal on top.

A few weeks after Mecca opened, the Muslim army marched out to meet the tribe of Hawazin. It was the biggest force they had ever gathered, around twelve thousand, and the early accounts say someone in the ranks said it out loud: we won't be beaten today for lack of numbers. You know the feeling. The team is stacked, the spreadsheet looks great, and a little voice in your chest says: we can't lose. Before dawn they went down into a narrow valley called Hunayn. The enemy was already hidden in the slopes above them.
screen: `THE BIGGEST ARMY YET.` → `WE CAN'T LOSE TODAY.` → `A NARROW VALLEY, BEFORE DAWN.`

segments.voice: The ambush broke over them in the half-dark: arrows from the slopes, the path too narrow to turn in. The great army ran. Camels bolted. Men scattered back up the valley. The Qur'an doesn't hide this. In the ninth surah it tells the believers, in Pickthall's words, that on the day of Hunayn, "ye exulted in your multitude but it availed you naught," and that the wide earth felt narrow to them, and they turned and fled. That's an honest scripture, remembering its own community's worst morning. In the middle of the panic, the hadith collections say, the Prophet ﷺ did not run. He stayed on his white mule, with a handful of companions around him, and called out who he was: I am the Prophet, that is no lie. His uncle al-'Abbas, who had a huge voice, shouted for the people to come back, and they came, turning their camels around. Then, the surah says, God sent down His sakinah, a calm, a peace of reassurance, on the Prophet and the believers, and the battle turned. Muslim teachers draw a simple lesson from Hunayn. The same people who had won at Badr when they were few almost lost when they were many. The difference wasn't the count; it was where their trust was resting. Numbers can be good. They just can't be God. After the battle, the reports add, he was generous even with the defeated tribe, and many of Hawazin became Muslims.
screen: `AMBUSH IN THE HALF-DARK.` · `YE EXULTED IN YOUR MULTITUDE.` · `HE STAYED, AND CALLED THEM BACK.` · `SAKINAH — CALM SENT DOWN.` · then, large: `NUMBERS DIDN'T HELP.`

segments.voice: Think of a number you lean on: followers, savings, years of experience, likes on a post, steps, grades. Notice how it feels to think about it, a little taller maybe, then imagine it at zero for a moment and notice what's still there. If you pray, you can place your trust back where Muslims say it belongs, with God; if you don't, just rest in whatever is left when the number is gone.
Sakinah, the calm sent down to the ones who stood, when the biggest army nearly broke in the valley of Hunayn.
Your line: numbers didn't help. The calm came to the ones who stood. Day two hundred eighty-one.

282.title: The march to Tabuk
282.hook: a long march in the heat, and three who stayed behind and told the truth (9:117–118)
282.howItsDone: Muslims read Ka'b ibn Malik's account in the hadith collections as a model of repentance through honesty, and 9:119, be with the truthful, is often quoted in sermons on truthfulness.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sakinah: the calm sent down to the ones who stood, when the biggest army yet nearly broke at Hunayn. Your line was numbers didn't help.

In the summer heat, the Prophet ﷺ called for a long march north to Tabuk, near the Byzantine frontier. Ka'b's own account says it came at a hard moment: fierce heat, a long distance, and the fruit in Medina just ripening, the shade at its best. A large army went. Some stayed home and later came with excuses. And one man, Ka'b ibn Malik, a veteran who had no excuse at all, kept telling himself he'd catch up tomorrow, and tomorrow, until the army was too far away. Missing something is one thing. Explaining it is another. The easy excuse is always right there: the car, the sick kid, the dead phone.
screen: `A MARCH IN FIERCE HEAT.` → `SOME CAME BACK WITH EXCUSES.` → `KA'B KEPT SAYING TOMORROW.`

segments.voice: Sahih al-Bukhari keeps Ka'b's account in his own voice, told years later. When the army returned, the people who had stayed behind lined up with their excuses, more than eighty of them, the report says, and the Prophet accepted what they said on the surface and left their hearts to God. Then it was Ka'b's turn. He was a good talker, he said later, and could have walked out of there with a story. Instead he told the truth: I had no excuse. I was never stronger or better off than when I stayed behind. The Prophet said: this one has told the truth. Two others, Murarah and Hilal, said the same. Then came the hard part. For fifty days, the community was told not to speak to the three. Ka'b would greet the Prophet and watch to see if his lips moved in reply. His cousin wouldn't answer him. The ninth surah describes it: the earth, vast as it was, became narrow for them, and their own souls felt narrow, until they understood there was no refuge from God except in Him. Then the verses came down: God had turned to them in forgiveness. Ka'b said afterward that the greatest blessing of his life, after Islam itself, was that he didn't lie that day. And the surah adds a line, in Pickthall's words: "be with the truthful."
screen: `KA'B TELLS IT HIMSELF.` · `I HAD NO EXCUSE.` · `FIFTY DAYS OF SILENCE.` · `GOD TURNED TO THEM.` · then, large: `BE WITH THE TRUTHFUL.`

segments.voice: Think of a small excuse you've been using: the reason you gave for missing something, the version of events that's a little kinder to you than it should be. Name the true version to yourself, plainly, the way Ka'b did: I had no excuse. If you pray, you can say it to God; if there's a person you owe the truth to, just notice who it is.
Sidq, truthfulness: what the three who stayed behind from the march to Tabuk told, even when it cost them fifty hard days.
Your line: the truth saved them. Fifty hard days, and then forgiveness. See you tomorrow.

283.title: The year of delegations
283.hook: tribes from all over Arabia come to Medina
283.howItsDone: Muslims honor guests as part of the sunnah, offering food, a place to rest and gifts, and surah an-Nasr (110), on people entering the religion in troops, is often taught alongside the story of this season.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sidq, and Ka'b, who could have talked his way out and said instead: I had no excuse. Your line was the truth saved them.

Bags in the hallway, someone always at the door, the kettle never cold. That's a house with guests for a week. Medina had a whole season of it. After Mecca opened and the army came back from Tabuk, the tribes of Arabia started arriving: from Yemen in the south, from the Gulf coast in the east, from the desert tribes and the mountain towns. Poets, chiefs, farmers, men who'd fought against him a year before. Muslim historians gave that stretch of time a name: wufud.
screen: `A HOUSE FULL OF GUESTS.` → `FROM YEMEN, THE GULF, THE DESERT.` → `THE YEAR OF DELEGATIONS.`

segments.voice: Some delegations came to accept Islam. Some came to make a treaty. Some came to look him over and argue. The Qur'an even records one group that stood outside his private rooms and shouted for him to come out, and it says gently that it would have been better if they had waited. That season, the Prophet ﷺ spent much of his time receiving them, and the reports say he received them well: he gave them a place to stay, fed them, and gave gifts when they left. One visit the biographers tell at length came from Najran, in the south: a delegation of Christians who came to talk about Jesus, long and hard. The early biographer Ibn Ishaq reports that when their time of prayer came, they prayed in the Prophet's mosque, and when some people moved to stop them, he said, let them. They went home with a treaty that protected their churches. Scholars discuss how strong that report is, but it's told and retold. A short surah that commentators connect with this season says, in Pickthall's words: "thou seest mankind entering the religion of Allah in troops." And what does it tell him to do at that moment of success? Praise his Lord, and ask forgiveness. Not a victory lap. Even at the very end, the hadith say, lying ill, one of his last instructions was to keep giving gifts to delegations the way he had. The door stayed open to the end.
screen: `TO ACCEPT, TO TREAT, TO ARGUE.` · `FED, HOUSED, GIVEN GIFTS.` · `THE CHRISTIANS OF NAJRAN.` · `ENTERING IN TROOPS.` · then, large: `THEY CAME FROM EVERYWHERE.`

segments.voice: Think of the next person who'll come to your door, your desk or your table: a neighbor, a new coworker, a friend of a friend, a delivery driver. Picture them arriving, and yourself stopping what you're doing, looking up, and offering one small gift: a glass of water, a real question, their name said warmly. If you pray, you can ask for an open door.
Wufud, delegations: tribes from every corner of Arabia came to Medina that year, and found the door open.

284.title: The farewell pilgrimage
284.hook: the Prophet ﷺ performs his one Hajj with a vast crowd
284.howItsDone: Muslims able to afford it and physically able are required to make the Hajj once in their lives; pilgrims enter ihram, men in two white unstitched cloths, and follow the rites the Prophet performed on his farewell pilgrimage, calling the talbiyah as they go.

segments.voice: Yesterday, wufud, when tribes came from every corner of Arabia and found the door open. Your line was they came from everywhere.

A photo of the Hajj looks like water moving: a sea of people around the Ka'ba, the men in the same two plain white cloths. Those rites go back to one journey. In the tenth year after the hijra, the Prophet ﷺ announced he was going to Mecca for the pilgrimage. It was the only Hajj he made after leaving Mecca, and word spread fast. People came from all over Arabia to go with him, so many that, the reports say, you could look to your right and left, in front and behind, and see only pilgrims.
screen: `A SEA OF WHITE.` → `HIS ONLY HAJJ.` → `PILGRIMS AS FAR AS THE EYE COULD SEE.`

segments.voice: Much of what's known comes from one long hadith in Sahih Muslim, told by a companion named Jabir, who walks through the pilgrimage step by step, almost like a travel diary. At a place outside Medina, the Prophet put on ihram, the state of the pilgrim; for the men, that meant two unstitched white cloths. A king and a shepherd look exactly the same in them. Then he began the talbiyah, and the crowd called it with him: labbayk, Allahumma, labbayk. Here I am, O God, here I am. Labbayk is the answer you give when someone calls your name and you come running. Jabir describes him circling the Ka'ba, walking between the hills of Safa and Marwah, standing at Arafah, throwing stones at Mina. Along the way, he said something that explains why Muslims still perform Hajj in almost exactly these steps: take your rites from me, for I may not make the pilgrimage again after this year. He was teaching by doing, and he seems to have known it was the last chance. That's why it's called the farewell pilgrimage. Today the men still wear the same two white cloths; women wear modest clothing, which may be white as well. And the call is the same one Jabir heard: here I am. All in white, all saying the same thing, all equal.
screen: `JABIR'S LONG HADITH.` · `IHRAM — KING AND SHEPHERD ALIKE.` · `LABBAYK — HERE I AM.` · `TAKE YOUR RITES FROM ME.` · then, large: `ALL IN WHITE.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes if you like and see the plain: a huge crowd, every person dressed the same, so you can't tell who's rich, who's famous, who's in charge. Now put yourself in it, in the same plain cloth, with nothing that marks you out, and notice what that feels like: lighter, maybe, or strange. If you pray, you can whisper the pilgrim's words, here I am; if you don't, just rest in the crowd.
Labbayk. The answer pilgrims called back to God during the Prophet's one Hajj, made with a vast crowd, not long before he died. Today's word.
Your line: all in white. No one in that crowd stood out above anyone else. Until tomorrow.

285.title: The farewell sermon
285.hook: lives and property sacred, women treated kindly, no Arab above non-Arab except by goodness
285.howItsDone: Muslims read and teach the farewell sermon, often in the days of Hajj and in Friday sermons, as a summary of the Prophet's message on the sacredness of life, the rights of women and the equality of people.

segments.voice: Yesterday, labbayk, the farewell pilgrimage's call: a vast crowd, the men in two plain cloths, all calling here I am. Your line was all in white.

If you had one last chance to talk to everyone who mattered to you, all at once, what would you say? Not the small stuff: the things you'd want them to hold on to after you were gone. On the plain of Arafah, during that one Hajj, the Prophet ﷺ sat on his camel and spoke. The crowd was so huge that, the biographers say, a man with a strong voice repeated his words outward, sentence by sentence, like ripples. Muslims call it the farewell sermon, and different parts of it are preserved in different hadith collections.
screen: `ONE LAST CHANCE TO SPEAK.` → `ON THE PLAIN OF ARAFAH.` → `WORDS REPEATED OUTWARD.`

segments.voice: First: your lives and your property are sacred to one another, as sacred as this day, in this month, in this city. He took the holiest time and place they knew and said: a person is that holy. Then he canceled the old blood feuds of the days before Islam, and the old debts of interest, and he began with his own family's claims. You can't ask others to drop their grudges if you keep yours. Then: fear God concerning women. He reminded the men that they had taken their wives on a trust from God, and that the women had rights over them, including to be provided for with kindness. And there's a line from a sermon during that pilgrimage, preserved in the Musnad of Imam Ahmad: no Arab has any superiority over a non-Arab, nor a non-Arab over an Arab, nor a white person over a Black person, nor a Black person over a white person, except by goodness, by taqwa, mindfulness of God. It echoes a verse of the Qur'an, in Pickthall's words: "O mankind! Lo! We have created you male and female, and have made you nations and tribes that ye may know one another." To know one another, not to rank one another. He told them he was leaving them the Book of God. Then he asked the crowd: have I conveyed it to you? They said yes. And he lifted his finger to the sky, pointed it toward the people, and said: O God, bear witness.
screen: `A PERSON IS AS SACRED AS THIS DAY.` · `HE CANCELED HIS OWN FAMILY'S CLAIMS FIRST.` · `FEAR GOD CONCERNING WOMEN.` · `NO ARAB ABOVE A NON-ARAB.` · then, large: `O GOD, BEAR WITNESS.`

segments.voice: Think of someone you tend to rank, even silently: above you, a boss, someone richer or cleverer; or below you, someone younger, poorer, newer, from somewhere you've judged. Picture them standing beside you on that plain, same height, same cloth, and hold them there, level, for a few breaths. If you pray, you can ask to see people as the sermon did.
Taqwa. Mindfulness of God — the one measure the Prophet gave for superiority among people, in his farewell sermon on the plain of Arafah. Today's word.
Your line: no one above another. Only goodness weighs, nothing else. That's day two hundred eighty-five.

286.title: "This day I have perfected"
286.hook: at Arafah the verse comes: this day I have perfected your religion (5:3)
286.howItsDone: Muslims hold the day of Arafah as one of the holiest of the year; many who are not on Hajj fast that day, and 5:3 is often recited to explain that the religion was completed in the Prophet's lifetime.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the farewell sermon on the plain of Arafah: every life sacred, and no Arab above a non-Arab except by goodness, by taqwa. Your line was no one above another.

On the day of Arafah, during that same Hajj, a Friday that year, a verse came down to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, twenty-three years after the first revelation in the cave. It's in the fifth surah, tucked into the middle of a passage about food. You know the feeling it names: something you've worked on for years is finally done. The last brick. The final page. You step back and look at it whole for the first time. It's joy, and something quieter too, because a thing that's finished also means a season is over.
screen: `ARAFAH, ON A FRIDAY.` → `TWENTY-THREE YEARS AFTER THE CAVE.` → `THE LAST BRICK.`

segments.voice: In Pickthall's translation, the verse reads: "This day have I perfected your religion for you and completed My favour unto you, and have chosen for you as religion AL-ISLAM." Three verbs, in order: perfected, completed, chosen. The Arabic behind perfected is akmaltu, from kamal, wholeness, the thing lacking nothing. Muslims understand the verse to mean the religion was now complete: its core teaching, its worship and its law were in place, and nothing essential would be added after the Prophet. That's one reason the sunnah matters so much, and why Muslim scholars are careful about new additions to worship. Sahih al-Bukhari keeps a striking conversation about this verse. A Jewish man told the caliph 'Umar: there's a verse in your book that, if it had come to us, we would have made that day a festival. 'Umar asked which one, and the man recited this verse. And 'Umar said: I know the day and the place it came down. It was at Arafah, on a Friday. As if to say: we already hold that day as a great one. A common mistake: this is not universally counted as the last verse revealed. Many scholars say a few other verses came after it, and they discuss which was truly last. What it marks is the whole being complete. And some companions heard sadness in it too. If the work is complete, the one who brought it may not stay much longer. Eighty-some days later, he was gone.
screen: `PERFECTED, COMPLETED, CHOSEN.` · `AKMALTU — NOTHING LACKING.` · `'UMAR: I KNOW THE DAY AND THE PLACE.` · `COMPLETE, NOT NECESSARILY LAST.` · then, large: `COMPLETED.`

segments.voice: At Uhud the line was hold the hill, staying at your post; today is the other half, the moment the work is done. Think of one small thing you've left almost done, the email drafted, the drawer half sorted, the thank-you you meant to send, and picture it complete: sent, sorted, said, whole. If you pray, you can give thanks for something in your life that is already complete.
Akmaltu. I have perfected — the verb in the verse at Arafah, from kamal, wholeness, telling Muslims their religion was complete. Today's word.
Your line: completed. Joy, and a quiet sense that a season is ending. See you tomorrow.

287.title: The illness
287.hook: he falls ill and is nursed in Aisha's room
287.howItsDone: Muslims count visiting the sick, 'iyadah, as a right owed between Muslims and a deed of great reward, and pray for the healing of the people they visit.

segments.voice: Yesterday, akmaltu, this day I have perfected: the verse at Arafah that said the religion was whole. Your line was completed.

A glass of water on the side table. Curtains half drawn. Voices lowered in the hall. A sickroom has the same hush in every century. Back in Medina, not long after the farewell pilgrimage, the Prophet ﷺ began to suffer from a severe headache and fever. It didn't pass. He kept going to the mosque as long as he could, and kept to his custom of spending each night with one of his wives in turn. But he grew weaker, and he kept asking, the reports say: where am I tomorrow?
screen: `A SICKBED IN MEDINA.` → `HEADACHE AND FEVER.` → `WHERE AM I TOMORROW?`

segments.voice: Sahih al-Bukhari tells it through Aisha. When the illness grew heavy, he asked his wives for permission to be nursed in her room, and they all agreed. Even sick, he asked. He walked there leaning on two men, his feet dragging a line in the dirt. That small room, next to the mosque, is where his last days happened. Companions came in and out. His daughter Fatimah came. Aisha nursed him. And all his life he had been the visitor at other people's sickbeds. The reports show him there again and again, and once, al-Bukhari says, at the bedside of a Jewish boy who had served him and fallen ill; he invited the boy to Islam, and the boy accepted. He listed visiting the sick among the rights one Muslim has over another. The Arabic for this visiting is 'iyadah. A hadith qudsi, words he reported from God, preserved in Sahih Muslim, takes it further. On the Day of Judgment, God will say: son of Adam, I was sick and you did not visit Me. The person says: how could I visit You, when You are the Lord of the worlds? And God says: my servant was sick and you did not visit him. Had you visited him, you would have found Me with him. It closes a week of hard lessons: numbers didn't help, the truth saved them, they came from everywhere, all in white, no one above another, completed. Now, the sickroom.
screen: `EVEN SICK, HE ASKED PERMISSION.` · `THE ROOM BESIDE THE MOSQUE.` · `HE HAD ALWAYS VISITED THE SICK.` · `YOU WOULD HAVE FOUND ME WITH HIM.` · then, large: `VISIT THE SICK.`

segments.voice: Who's unwell in your life right now: someone in the hospital, someone whose illness has gone on so long people have stopped asking, someone recovering at home, someone struggling in their mind? Picture them and the room they're in, and choose how you'd reach them: a visit, a call, a message, a meal left at the door. If you pray, you can pray for their healing now.
The illness. The Prophet's last sickness, nursed in Aisha's room, and a reminder of how he always visited the sick. Today's word.
Your line: visit the sick. Five minutes of your voice may be the best part of their day. That's day two hundred eighty-seven.
